name: root vegetable tian
notes:
Red onions are not optional.

GREEN APPLES (GRANNY SMITH OR SIMILAR): use green apples specifically — the tart-firm character holds up to the bake and reads better against the earthy root vegetables and gruyere than sweet varieties (honey crisp, gala) would. Sliced or thinly wedged and arranged alongside the root vegetables in the tian.

CINNAMON + NUTMEG: warm-spice pair that ties the apples to the roots and the cheese. A pinch of each is enough — don't overdo, this is savory-adjacent-with-warmth, not a dessert.

BUTTER + OLIVE OIL: butter carries dairy richness that pairs with the gruyere; olive oil provides bulk fat and keeps the butter from burning at the high oven temp. Same split logic as marcella-frittata and other cookbook recipes where butter is flavor and oil is volume.

PARSLEY: chopped fresh, scattered on top after the bake. Off-heat green herbal finish against the browned cheese-topped tian.

FAILURE MODE — TOO MUCH OIL: the butter + olive oil combo is great for flavor but watch the total amount. The gruyere leaks its own fat as it melts, so the finished tian ends up with more fat than the fats-you-added-during-prep math suggests. Start conservative on both butter and oil — you can always drizzle more later, but there's no fix for a greasy tian.

SKIP THE ONION SAUTE — NOT NEEDED: I used to pre-sauté the red onions before adding them to the tian. Skipping that step is the current best-move call. The onions bake alongside the root vegetables and soften enough on their own during the oven time. Saves a step and a pan.

COVERED VS UNCOVERED BAKE — LIDLESS IS THE MOVE (COVERED GOES SOGGY, NO FIX): still working through this but leaning firmly toward all-uncovered. When I've tried a covered-then-uncovered bake (steaming the roots through under a lid before uncovering to brown), the tian goes soggy and NO amount of post-uncover baking recovers the mush. This is the same issue as the italian-tomato-white-beans tian in reverse — that recipe wants the covered bake because it has a liquid bean base that steams the eggplant on top; here there's no liquid base and the covered step just traps moisture from the vegetables in the pan without a positive purpose. Bake uncovered from start to finish.
why_i_like_this_recipe: It's a really unique way to use carrots — eat them baked/whole with spices and cheese (normally carrots are just sautee fodder). Also a great reason to buy celery root. And an excuse to buy gruyere cheese.
